newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Ratsiraka takes lead in Madagascar early returns.
newsitem.headline: Ratsiraka takes lead in Madagascar early returns.

text.p: Former Marxist military ruler Didier Ratsiraka took a strong lead over ex-president Albert Zafy in early returns in a run-off presidential election on Sunday in the Indian Ocean island republic of Madagascar.
The first votes to be tallied, cast in the capital Antananarivo, gave Ratsiraka about 65 percent to 35 percent for Zafy.
No returns were yet available from polling stations outside of the capital area, and full results were not expected for several days because of poor communications in many areas.
But an opinion poll taken shortly before Sunday's run-off showed Ratsiraka with 60 percent to 40 percent for Zafy.
Political analysts were predicting that Ratsiraka, a 60-year-old retired admiral, would carry four of Madagascar's six provinces.
The two where Zafy was believed stronger were Antsiranana in northern Madagascar and Toliara in the south, both of which are less populous compared to the rest of the island, analysts said.
Most of Madagascar's 6.5 million eligible voters failed to take part in Sunday's run-off, election officials said.
An estimated two-thirds of those eligible to cast a ballot had stayed away from polling stations, they said.

The vote in the Indian Ocean island republic was called after Zafy, 69, elected to succeed Ratsiraka in 1993, was impeached by parliament in July for abuse of his authority and exceeding his constitutional powers.
Zafy had earlier won a referendum empowering him, rather than parliament, to appoint the prime minister.
Ratsiraka returned from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September, after a campaign that aroused little excitement.
None of the 15 candidates in the first round in November won the necessary 50 per cent of votes to secure outright victory.
Ratsiraka led the first-round poll with 36.6 per cent of the vote, against 23.4 per cent for Zafy.
In a radio interview on Sunday Ratsiraka said he was confident of victory but would support Zafy if he lost.
Sale of alcohol was banned for the day, and observers from francophone African countries were monitoring the polls, which closed at 6 p.m. (1500 GMT).
He was reviled by many of his people in the early 1990s for using the army to resist the pro-democracy movement in Madagascar, where most of the population of 14 million live in chronic poverty.
His ousting in 1993 followed a wave of political protest which virtually paralysed the country for many months.

Diplomats said the optimism that marked Ratsiraka's ousting had evaporated in the political squabbling after Zafy took over, and many people apparently thought they would be better off with Ratsiraka back in office.
